title: High-stakes sports gambler pleads guilty in CBA, NCAA game-fixing and NBA betting scheme
text:
← Back to the wire
High-stakes sports gambler pleads guilty in CBA, NCAA game-fixing and NBA betting scheme
Shane Hennen has pleaded guilty in federal court following involvement in schemes fixing basketball games across multiple leagues—including CBA, NCAA Division I, and NBA-related betting conspiracies—and now awaits sentencing facing decades of potential imprisonment.
Shane Hennen, also known as “Sugar Shane,” pleaded guilty on Oct. 15 to charges related to bribery in sporting contests, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and three counts of wire fraud before United States District Judge Nitza I. Quiñones Alejandro in Philadelphia. The plea stems from a years-long scheme involving the fixing of Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) games and National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) men’s Division I basketball games.
Hennen was charged by indictment earlier this year in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania for his role in recruiting and bribing players to influence or fix games through point-shaving during the 2022-2023 CBA season. According to court filings, Hennen’s main responsibility was placing bets and arranging for others to place large wagers against teams whose players had been bribed.
After profiting from CBA game-fixing activities, Hennen and co-conspirators targeted NCAA men’s basketball during the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 seasons. They agreed to recruit NCAA players willing to accept bribes for influencing game outcomes, particularly ensuring their team failed to cover the spread either for the first half or entire game. In total, more than 39 players across over 17 different NCAA Division I teams were involved in fixing or attempting to fix more than 29 games. The fraudulent activity resulted in over $3 million wagered on these games and financial losses exceeding $1.1 million for sportsbooks nationwide.
In a separate case prosecuted by superseding indictment in May in the Eastern District of New York, Hennen pleaded guilty to conspiracy charges relating both to wire fraud and money laundering connected with NBA betting schemes. Conspirators obtained insider information from several NBA players and coaches, which they used—through a network including Hennen—to place bets using confidential team data while falsely representing compliance with sportsbook rules.
The investigations were conducted by FBI Philadelphia with assistance from FBI New York and other agencies for the CBA/NCAA case; FBI New York and the New York Police Department investigated the NBA betting matter. Assistant United States Attorneys Louis D. Lappen and Jerome M. Maiatico are prosecuting for Pennsylvania.
Hennen is scheduled for sentencing on February 25 in Philadelphia, where he faces up to 85 years’ imprisonment plus fines and restitution on Pennsylvania charges; he also faces up to 40 years’ imprisonment plus additional penalties under federal prosecution out of New York.
